segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole inhabited world should be registered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (This was the first registration, made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.)

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And everyone went to be registered, each to his own town.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the town of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to be registered with Mary, who was betrothed to him and was pregnant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and she gave birth to her firstborn son. She swaddled him and laid him in a manger, because there was no space for them in the guest room.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same region there were shepherds living out in the fields and keeping the night watches over their flock.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The angel said to them,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Do not be afraid; for look, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people:

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: today in the town of David a Savior has been born for you, who is the Messiah, the Lord.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And this will be the sign for you: you will find a baby swaddled and lying in a manger.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people with whom he is pleased.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds began saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let us go over to Bethlehem, then, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had seen it, they made known the word that had been spoken to them about this child.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all who heard were amazed at what the shepherds told them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Mary treasured all these things, pondering them in her heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, just as it had been told to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When eight days were completed for his circumcision, he was given the name Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the days of their purification were completed according to the law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written in the law of the Lord,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what the custom of the law required,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simeon himself took him in his arms and blessed God and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Now you are releasing your slave, Master, according to your word, in peace;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for my eyes have seen your salvation,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: which you have prepared in the sight of all the peoples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for your people Israel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His father and mother were amazed at what was being said about him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that is spoken against—

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and a sword will pass through your own soul too—so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was also Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was far advanced in years, having lived with a husband for seven years after her marriage,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She never left the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayers night and day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to God and kept speaking about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had carried out everything required by the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town, Nazareth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favor of God was upon him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every year his parents went to Jerusalem for the festival of Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the festival,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when the days were over and they started back, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Assuming he was in the traveling party, they went a day’s journey and then began looking for him among their relatives and acquaintances.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, looking for him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When his parents saw him they were astounded, and his mother said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Child, why have you done this to us? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they did not understand the word he spoke to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. His mother kept all these things in her heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and people.

notes.phrase: when Quirinius was governor of Syria
notes.traditional: when Quirinius was governor of Syria
notes.note: Quirinius is known to have become governor of Syria in AD 6 and to have held a census of Judea then, about ten years after the death of Herod the Great, in whose reign Luke 1:5 and Matthew place Jesus’ birth. Proposed solutions include an earlier, otherwise unattested term of office for Quirinius, or translating ‘this registration was before Quirinius governed Syria’, which most grammarians find strained. The rendering here is the natural sense of the Greek; the historical difficulty is real and unresolved.

In Israel’s Scriptures ‘the city of David’ normally means the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem. Luke applies the phrase to Bethlehem, the village David came from, linking the birth to the hope for a ruler from David’s line. The same Greek word is used here for Nazareth and Bethlehem and is rendered ‘town’ throughout, since neither was a city in the modern sense.

The Greek word means a place to stay and is not the usual term for a commercial inn, for which Luke uses a different word in 10:34; in 22:11 he uses this word for the guest room of the Last Supper. Many scholars therefore picture a crowded guest room or lodging in a private house, with the baby laid where the animals were fed. The traditional ‘inn’ remains possible, and the exact kind of lodging cannot be settled.

The Greek christos here is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, so it is rendered ‘Messiah’, as in several modern translations; ‘Christ’ is kept where the word works as a name. The pairing of the two titles without articles is unusual and could also be read ‘an anointed Lord’. Verse 26 has the more common expression, ‘the Lord’s Messiah’.

‘Host’ is an old English word for an army, and the Greek word is an ordinary term for a military force. The Septuagint uses the phrase for the ranks of heavenly beings that attend God. With ‘host’ a modern reader can miss that it is an army that announces peace.

notes.phrase: among people with whom he is pleased
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read ‘people of good pleasure’, while later manuscripts differ by one letter and give the familiar ‘peace, good will toward men’. Most scholars accept the earlier reading. Similar Hebrew and Aramaic phrases in the Dead Sea Scrolls indicate that it refers to people on whom God’s favor rests, not to people who have good will.

Leviticus 12 prescribes purification for the mother alone, forty days after the birth of a son; the consecration of a firstborn son (Exodus 13) was a separate obligation. Luke’s ‘their’ is unexpected and has been taken to mean Mary and Joseph, or mother and child, or to be a loose combination of the two rites; a few manuscripts and versions alter it to ‘his’ or ‘her’. The offering of two birds in verse 24 is the one Leviticus allows for those who cannot afford a lamb.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: the same adjective can be translated ‘righteous’ or ‘just’, and the related noun ‘righteousness’ or ‘justice’. Here it describes a person who lives rightly before God, and the traditional ‘righteous’ is kept.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, and Simeon addresses God with the word for a slave’s owner (‘Master’, often rendered ‘Lord’). The verb means to release or dismiss and was also used of letting someone die. Most translations have ‘servant’ and ‘let depart’. In the Septuagint, ‘slave’ of God is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David.

The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then rendered ‘Gentiles’. It is one word in Greek, translated ‘nation’ or ‘Gentiles’ according to sense. Here it is set beside ‘your people Israel’, echoing Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6.

notes.phrase: as a widow until she was eighty-four
notes.traditional: a widow of about fourscore and four years
notes.note: The Greek can mean either that Anna lived as a widow up to the age of eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years, which would make her over a hundred. Most translations take the first reading, as here. The second is grammatically possible.

The Greek says literally ‘in the things of my Father’, with no noun expressed. Most modern scholars take it as an idiom for being at someone’s house, which suits the setting in the temple. The older rendering ‘about my Father’s business’ is also possible, as is ‘among those who belong to my Father’.

The Greek word can mean either bodily height or age and maturity. ‘Stature’ follows the traditional reading; several modern translations have ‘in years’ instead. The verse echoes the description of the boy Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26.

candidates.reason: Translations split between ‘servant’ and ‘slave’ across Gospels, letters and Revelation, and the choice affects how readers hear both parables and self-descriptions such as ‘slave of Christ’.
The word is rendered ‘grace’, ‘favor’ or ‘thanks’ by different translators, and it needs one policy on when ‘grace’ is kept and when ‘favor’ is used.
It recurs throughout the New Testament meaning life, self or inner person, and ‘soul’ can mislead where no immaterial part of a person is in view.
It is used of children, wives, slaves, citizens and Christ, and translators vary between ‘submit’, ‘be subject’ and ‘obey’ in ways readers will notice.
Greek distinguishes the temple complex (ἱερόν) from the sanctuary building (ναός), and a decision is needed on whether English marks that difference consistently.
